title: Public Space and the Right to Skate
bigQuestion: Who gets to use a city's shared spaces, and how have skaters won a place in them?

story.title: Maps on Poster Board
story.kicker: Skaters fill a council chamber and ask for a place of their own.
paragraphs: The city council chamber holds about eighty folding chairs, and on this Tuesday night every one is taken. Many of the people in them are teenagers. Some hold skateboards on their laps. Others hold sheets of poster board covered in marker drawings, arrows and colored dots.

The dots mark where people skate now. There are clusters at the library steps, the bank plaza and the parking deck behind the grocery store. A girl in the second row points to a red dot by the courthouse. Last month a security guard told her group to leave it. The next week, small metal knobs appeared on the ledge.

When public comment opens, a seventeen-year-old walks to the microphone. His hands shake a little. He explains that the nearest skatepark is a forty-minute bus ride away. He holds up a map with a green circle around an empty lot beside the community center. "We drew where we already go," he says. "This is the spot that would keep us off the courthouse ledge."

A shop owner speaks next. She says skaters have chipped her planters and startled her customers. A parent follows her and says skating is the only thing that got her son outside after a hard year. A council member asks how much a concrete park costs and who would be responsible if someone got hurt.

No vote happens that night. The council asks staff to study the empty lot and report back in two months. On the way out, the skaters stack the poster boards in the hallway. One of them writes the date of the next meeting on the back of every map.
story.think: Each speaker at the meeting wanted something different. Whose concerns would you need to answer to get a skatepark built?

lessons.title: Knobs on the Ledge
lessons.mainIdea: Skate stoppers are metal or stone pieces fixed to ledges, rails and benches to block grinding and sliding.
reading: Walk through a downtown plaza in almost any large city and look closely at the edges of the low walls. You may see small metal knobs, brackets or bumps bolted along the top every meter or so. These are *skate stoppers*. They break up a smooth edge so a skateboard truck or deck cannot slide along it.

Skate stoppers spread in the 1990s and 2000s, after street skating became the main way many people rode. Street skaters use the city as their terrain. A marble ledge, a handrail or a bench becomes a place to grind, which means scraping the metal trucks along an edge. A *ledge* is any long, flat-topped edge low enough to skate onto.

Building owners put in stoppers for several reasons. Grinding can chip stone and scrape paint. Skaters rub *wax* on ledges so boards slide more easily, and the wax leaves dark streaks. Owners also worry about noise, about people walking by, and about being blamed if someone is injured on their property. A stopper costs far less than replacing a damaged stone edge.

words.d: a knob, bracket or bump fixed to a ledge, rail or bench so a skateboard cannot grind or slide along it
a long, flat-topped edge, such as a low wall or planter, that skaters grind or slide on
a slippery substance skaters rub on an edge so the board slides with less friction

look.title: Two Ledges Side by Side
look.text: Picture two granite planters in front of an office building. The first has a smooth, square top edge, rubbed dark with wax. The second has the same edge, but a steel bracket shaped like a small shark fin is bolted to it every 90 centimeters. A skater rolls up to the first and slides the whole length. At the second, the skater stops, looks, and rides on.
look.prompt: List one reason the building owner chose the brackets and one thing the city loses when the smooth edge disappears.

choices: a piece fixed to an edge so a board cannot grind or slide on it
a brake on the back truck of a skateboard
a city law that bans skateboarding downtown
a ramp that slows skaters before a ledge
check.why: A skate stopper is a knob or bracket fixed to a ledge, rail or bench to block grinding and sliding.

check.q: Why do skaters rub wax on a ledge?
choices: so the ledge looks cleaner to owners
so the board slides with less friction
so the stone does not crack in cold weather
so the trucks grip the edge harder
check.why: Wax lowers friction, so the board slides farther along the edge.

check.q: Which is one reason building owners give for adding skate stoppers?
choices: Stoppers make ledges easier to grind.
Stoppers are required on every bench by federal law.

check.why: Owners point to chipped stone, wax streaks, noise and worries about injuries.

lessons.title: Hostile Design in the City
lessons.mainIdea: Hostile design shapes public objects to stop certain uses, and skate stoppers are one example among many.
reading: Skate stoppers belong to a larger family of city features. Planners and critics call this family *hostile design*, also known as defensive architecture. It means shaping a public object so that some people cannot use it in certain ways. The object still looks like a bench or a wall, but its shape quietly says no.

Common examples sit in plain sight. A bench may have armrests every half meter so no one can lie down. A ledge may slope so no one can sit. Spikes or rough stones may fill the space under a bridge. Bright lights or high-pitched sound devices may be aimed at places where teenagers gather.

People argue about these designs. Supporters say owners have a right to protect property and keep spaces clean and calm. Critics say the designs push away people who are already unwelcome elsewhere, such as unhoused people and young people with nowhere to go. They also note that a feature aimed at one group can make a space worse for everyone, such as an older person who needs a flat place to rest.

Skaters entered this debate because they are easy to see and hear. A *public space* is land or a place that anyone may enter, such as a sidewalk, park or plaza. When a city adds stoppers to a public plaza, it is choosing who that space is mainly for. Asking who decides, and why, is a central question in city planning.

words.d: shaping a public object, such as a bench or ledge, so that certain people cannot use it in certain ways; also called defensive architecture
a place anyone may enter and use, such as a sidewalk, park or plaza
another name for hostile design

look.title: One Bench, Three Users
look.text: A new bench at a bus stop has three seats split by metal armrests. A commuter sits and waits for the bus. An older man who feels dizzy wants to lie down for a minute but cannot. A skater who wanted to slide the bench's edge finds a bolted bump in the middle. One design choice changed the bench for all three people.
look.prompt: Who benefits from the armrests, and who loses something? Explain how a designer could balance those needs.

check.q: What does hostile design mean?
choices: building a skatepark with steep walls
painting city buildings in dark colors
designing a skateboard for street tricks
shaping public objects so some people cannot use them in certain ways
check.why: Hostile design, or defensive architecture, shapes objects to stop certain uses.

check.q: Which is an example of hostile design that is NOT aimed at skaters?
choices: armrests placed so no one can lie on a bench
a smooth concrete bowl
a waxed ledge in a skatepark
a painted curb at a skate plaza
check.why: Armrests that stop people from lying down are a common example of hostile design.

check.q: What do critics say about hostile design?
choices: It always makes public spaces safer for every user.
It pushes away people who already have few places to go and can make spaces worse for everyone.
It costs nothing and has no effect on people.
It was invented by skaters to protect ledges.
check.why: Critics argue it pushes out unhoused and young people and can hurt other users, such as older people needing rest.

lessons.title: Why a Stopper Throws a Rider
lessons.mainIdea: When a stopper halts the board, the rider's body keeps moving forward, and wax works by lowering friction.
reading: Imagine a skater sliding along a ledge at 3 meters per second when the board hits a bolted knob. The board stops in a few centimeters. The skater's body does not. It keeps moving forward at about 3 meters per second until the ground, a hand or a knee stops it. This is *inertia*: an object keeps its motion unless a force changes it.

Isaac Newton stated this as the first law of motion in his Principia in 1687. A skate stopper applies a large force to the board for a very short time. Nothing applies that force to the rider's chest and head. That is why a hidden stopper is dangerous, and why skaters scout a spot before they ride it.

Wax works on the other side of the problem. When a board slides on a ledge, kinetic friction slows it. On a level edge the friction force is f = μN, where N is the board and rider's weight, and the slowing is μg. The slide distance before stopping is v² ÷ (2μg). The *coefficient of friction*, μ, is a number that describes how grippy two surfaces are together.

Here is a worked example with v = 3 m/s and g = 9.8 m/s². On a bare edge with an example μ of 0.5, the distance is 9 ÷ (2 × 0.5 × 9.8) = 9 ÷ 9.8, about 0.92 m. With wax, suppose μ drops to 0.2. Then 9 ÷ (2 × 0.2 × 9.8) = 9 ÷ 3.92, about 2.3 m. Lower friction more than doubles the slide, which is why skaters wax and why owners see streaks.

words.d: the tendency of an object to keep moving, or keep still, unless a force changes its motion
a number, written μ, that describes how strongly two surfaces resist sliding over each other
the friction force that slows an object already sliding; on a level surface it equals μ times the weight

look.title: Slide Distance at 3 m/s
look.cite: Worked example using d = v²/(2μg) with v = 3 m/s and g = 9.8 m/s²; μ values are examples
look.prompt: By how many meters does going from μ = 0.5 to μ = 0.2 lengthen the slide?

check.q: A board hits a skate stopper and stops. Why does the rider keep going?
choices: The stopper pushes the rider forward.
Gravity pulls the rider forward along the ledge.
Inertia: the body keeps its motion until a force stops it.
Wax on the ledge speeds the rider up.
check.why: Newton's first law says the body keeps moving until a force changes its motion.

check.q: Using d = v²/(2μg) with v = 3 m/s, μ = 0.5 and g = 9.8 m/s², about how far does the board slide?
What does wax change in the slide-distance formula?
choices: It lowers μ, so the distance gets longer.
It raises g, so the board falls faster.
It raises the speed v at the start.
It doubles the weight N.
check.why: Wax lowers the coefficient of friction μ, and a smaller μ gives a longer slide.

lessons.title: A Concrete Space in London
lessons.mainIdea: Skaters have used the undercroft beneath London's Southbank Centre since the 1970s, making it one of the oldest skate spots still in use.
reading: On the south bank of the River Thames in central London stands a group of concrete arts buildings from the late 1960s, part of the Southbank Centre. Beneath one of them is a wide, covered, open-sided space with low banks, steps and pillars. This space is called the *undercroft*, an old word for a room or vault under a building.

Skaters found the undercroft in the 1970s. Its smooth concrete, its gentle slopes and its roof against London rain made it useful all year. It was never designed for skateboarding. Skaters adopted it, the way street skaters adopt any good surface. Over the decades BMX riders, graffiti writers and photographers made it their home too.

The undercroft's buildings are an example of *Brutalism*, a style of architecture that leaves raw concrete exposed in large, blocky shapes. Many people disliked the style. Skaters, though, valued exactly what others found harsh: hard, smooth, durable surfaces. Generations of British skaters learned there, and visitors from around the world came to see it.

words.d: a covered space or vault beneath a building; at Southbank, the skated space under the arts center
a style of architecture with raw, exposed concrete in large, blocky shapes, popular from the 1950s to the 1970s
a group of arts buildings on the south bank of the River Thames in London

look.title: Reading the Undercroft
look.text: Picture a long, low space under a concrete building, open on the river side. The floor is smooth and grey. Short concrete banks rise toward the back wall. Square pillars hold up the ceiling. Painted words cover the walls. Rain falls on the walkway outside, but the floor inside stays dry. A skater rolls down one bank and up the next.
look.prompt: Name three features of this space that make it good for skating, and explain why each one matters.

check.q: Since about when have skaters used the Southbank undercroft?
choices: the 1920s
the 1970s
the 1990s
check.why: Skaters have used the undercroft since the 1970s.

check.q: What is an undercroft?
choices: a ramp built of plywood
a kind of skateboard wheel
a covered space or vault beneath a building
a park beside a river
check.why: An undercroft is a covered space under a building.

check.q: Why did skaters value the Brutalist concrete at Southbank?
choices: It was built as a skatepark with ramps and rails.
It was painted bright colors for skaters.
It was the only building in London with stairs.
Its hard, smooth surfaces were durable and good to ride, and the roof kept off rain.
check.why: The smooth concrete and roof made it skateable year round, though it was not designed for skating.

lessons.title: Long Live Southbank
lessons.mainIdea: When a redevelopment plan threatened the undercroft, the Long Live Southbank campaign won an agreement in 2014 to keep it.
reading: In 2013 the Southbank Centre announced plans to redevelop its buildings. The plans would have turned the undercroft into shops and restaurants. Skaters would have been offered a new space under a nearby bridge instead. The centre argued the new shops would help pay for repairs to the old buildings.

Skaters and supporters formed a *campaign*, an organized effort to win a goal. They called it Long Live Southbank. They argued that the undercroft's value came from its history and the community built there, and that a new space could not simply replace it. They gathered petitions, filed objections to the planning application and spoke to the press and to local officials.

In 2014 the campaign and the Southbank Centre reached an agreement that the undercroft would stay where it was, for skating. The campaign later raised money to help restore parts of the space that had been closed off. Long Live Southbank showed that skaters could use the ordinary tools of civic life, such as petitions, planning objections and public meetings, to protect a place.

The case also raised a wider idea. *Heritage* usually means old buildings, monuments and art that a society chooses to protect. Southbank skaters argued that a living community and its way of using a place can be heritage too, even if the use was never planned.

words.d: an organized effort by a group of people to reach a goal, such as saving a place or changing a decision
places, objects and ways of life that a community values and chooses to protect for the future
rebuilding or changing an area or building for a new use

look.title: Two Plans for One Space
look.text: Plan A: the undercroft becomes a row of restaurants, and skaters get a new, purpose-built space a short walk away under a bridge. Plan B: the undercroft stays as it is, and the arts center looks for repair money elsewhere. Both plans give skaters somewhere to ride. The campaign chose to fight for Plan B.
look.prompt: Explain why the campaign rejected a new space, using the idea of heritage in your answer.

check.why: The agreement to keep the undercroft for skating came in 2014.

check.why: The plan would have filled the undercroft with shops and restaurants and offered skaters a space under a nearby bridge.

check.q: Which tools did the campaign use?

check.why: Long Live Southbank used ordinary civic tools such as petitions and planning objections.

lessons.title: Burnside Under the Bridge
lessons.mainIdea: In 1990 skaters in Portland, Oregon, began building a concrete park under the Burnside Bridge without permission, and the city later accepted it.
reading: Under the east end of the Burnside Bridge in Portland, Oregon, there was a patch of dirt and broken ground that few people used. In 1990 a group of local skaters started pouring concrete there. They bought bags of cement, mixed it, and shaped banks against the bridge's walls. Nobody had given them permission.

The skaters kept building, a section at a time, using money they raised themselves. They also cleared trash and discouraged drug dealing in the area. Over time the city decided to accept the park instead of tearing it out. Burnside became one of the most famous skateparks in the world, known for steep, rough, hand-shaped concrete.

Building on land you do not own is *trespassing*, and it can lead to fines or removal. Burnside's story worked out partly because the land was neglected, the skaters improved it, and neighbors and officials came to see the benefit. Many other skater-built spots have been torn down. Burnside is famous as an exception, not a guarantee.

words.d: going onto or using land or property without the owner's permission
a skater-built concrete skatepark under the Burnside Bridge in Portland, Oregon, begun in 1990
a flat, sloped surface that skaters ride up and down, like a tilted wall

check.why: Building without permission is trespassing; many such spots are removed, so Burnside's acceptance is unusual.

lessons.title: The Do-It-Yourself Spirit
lessons.mainIdea: DIY skate spots grow from skaters building what their city lacks, and safe building takes skill, planning and permission.
reading: Skaters use the letters *DIY*, for do-it-yourself, to describe spots they build with their own hands. A DIY spot might be one small concrete bank against a wall, a painted curb, or a whole park like Burnside. The idea goes back to the 1970s, when skaters drained backyard pools and built wooden ramps in driveways.

DIY spots tend to grow where public parks are missing or far away. They also reflect taste. Skaters who build their own terrain can make it steeper, rougher or stranger than a city would. Many DIY builders later used what they learned to start companies that design and build public skateparks.

Building with concrete is real construction work. Wet cement can burn skin, so builders wear gloves, long sleeves and eye protection. Bags of cement are heavy, and a poorly shaped transition can throw a rider. The safest way for a young skater to take part is to join a group that has permission from the landowner, works with experienced builders and adults, and follows local rules.

A legal path also exists. Some cities now let skaters help design or even build public parks with official approval. This keeps the creativity of DIY while removing the risk that the spot will be bulldozed a month later. It also means the city inspects the work and can take care of the park for years.

words.d: do-it-yourself; in skating, a spot that skaters build themselves
the curved part of a ramp or bowl that joins the flat ground to a wall
the shapes and surfaces a skater rides, such as banks, ledges, rails and bowls

look.title: A Legal Build Day
look.text: On a Saturday morning, a parks department worker unlocks a gate at a small public lot. Twelve skaters and two experienced concrete builders arrive. Everyone puts on gloves and safety glasses. The builders explain the plan: one low bank, shaped against an existing wall. The younger skaters carry tools, rake gravel and smooth edges while the builders mix and pour.

check.why: DIY stands for do-it-yourself; skaters use it for spots they build.

check.q: Why do builders wear gloves and long sleeves around wet cement?
choices: Cement is magnetic and pulls on tools.
Gloves make the concrete dry faster.
Long sleeves keep the concrete smooth.

check.why: Wet cement can burn skin, so builders cover their hands and arms.

check.q: What is the safest way for a young skater to help build a spot?
choices: join a group with landowner permission, experienced builders and adults

check.why: Permission, experienced builders and adults make the work safer and the spot more likely to last.

lessons.title: Paying for Public Parks
lessons.mainIdea: The Tony Hawk Foundation, founded in 2002 and renamed The Skatepark Project in 2020, helps communities build public skateparks.
reading: Tony Hawk, the skater famous for landing the first 900 at the 1999 X Games, started the Tony Hawk Foundation in 2002. Its goal was to help communities build free, public skateparks, especially in places with few resources. A *public skatepark* is one owned by a city or park district and open to anyone, usually without a fee.

The foundation gave grants, which are gifts of money for a specific project that do not have to be paid back. Just as important, it gave advice. Many city officials had never planned a skatepark. The foundation shared guidance on choosing a site, involving local skaters, picking an experienced designer and building with long-lasting concrete.

In 2020 the organization changed its name to The Skatepark Project. The new name put the focus on the parks and the communities rather than on one famous person. Over its history it has helped fund many hundreds of parks across the United States. Its work shows a shift from skaters fighting cities to skaters working with them.

words.d: a gift of money for a specific project that does not have to be paid back
a skatepark owned by a city or park district and open to anyone, usually for free
the name since 2020 of the Tony Hawk Foundation, founded in 2002 to help build public skateparks

One leader wants a cheap kit of metal ramps from a catalog. A local skater suggests a smaller concrete park designed with input from the people who will ride it.
look.prompt: Which choice fits the advice skatepark groups give, and why might concrete be worth waiting for?

lessons.title: Reasons for Skateparks
lessons.mainIdea: Supporters say skateparks give young people a safe, free place to be active and build community, away from traffic and private property.
reading: People who want a skatepark usually make four kinds of arguments. The first is safety. A park gives skaters smooth ground away from cars, which removes one of the most serious dangers of riding in streets and parking lots. The second is fairness. Cities already build ball fields, courts and pools; supporters argue that skaters deserve space too.

The third argument is health and belonging. Skating is exercise, and it does not need a team, a coach, a schedule or a fee. A teenager who did not fit into team sports can find a group at the park. Older skaters often teach younger ones, so a park can work like an informal classroom.

The fourth argument is about the rest of the city. A good park gives skaters a better place to ride than a courthouse ledge or a store's planters. Business owners who complain about skaters often become supporters once skaters have somewhere else to go. Supporters use the word *stakeholder* for anyone with something to gain or lose from a decision, and they try to show that a park helps several stakeholders at once.

words.d: a person or group with something to gain or lose from a decision
a reason, backed by facts, offered to persuade others
a place built for skateboarding, with features such as ramps, bowls, ledges and rails

look.title: Matching Reasons to Listeners
look.text: At a hearing, three people will vote: a council member who worries about budgets, one who worries about crime, and one who worries about teenagers' health. A skater has two minutes to speak. She has notes on traffic safety, free exercise, older skaters mentoring younger ones and fewer complaints from downtown shops.
look.prompt: Pick one reason for each council member and explain why that reason fits that listener.

check.why: Supporters say parks remove the danger of riding near traffic.

check.why: A stakeholder is anyone affected by a decision.

check.why: A park can draw skaters away from private property that owners worry about.

lessons.title: Concerns About Parks and Streets
lessons.mainIdea: Opponents raise cost, noise, injury and property damage, and skaters debate whether parks should replace street skating.
reading: Not everyone wants a skatepark nearby. Neighbors worry about noise from wheels and boards slapping concrete, especially in the evening. Officials worry about cost, since a well-built concrete park is a real construction project. Some worry about *liability*, which is legal responsibility if someone gets hurt. Several U.S. states have passed laws that limit a city's liability for injuries at public skateparks, and that has made parks easier to approve.

Street skating raises sharper concerns. Skaters can chip ledges, scratch rails and leave wax on stone. Pedestrians may feel unsafe when boards move quickly past them. Skating on private property without permission is trespassing. Many cities ban skating on certain sidewalks or plazas, and police may issue tickets.

Skaters argue among themselves too. Some say parks are a gift that keeps riders safe. Others say a park can become a fence: once it exists, a city may feel free to ban skating everywhere else. Street skaters value the challenge of real architecture, and some of the most creative tricks in skating's history were done on ordinary city objects.

A middle path has grown since the 2000s. Some cities now build *skate plazas*, which look like ordinary public plazas with ledges, steps and benches but are made to be skated. Other cities mark a few downtown spots where skating is allowed. These ideas treat skaters as one group of users sharing a space, rather than a problem to remove.

words.d: legal responsibility for harm, such as an injury on someone's property
a public space built to look like a city plaza, with ledges, steps and benches made for skating
skating on everyday city features such as curbs, ledges, steps and rails rather than in a park

look.title: One Plaza, Shared
look.text: A city rebuilds its library plaza. The granite ledges are made thicker, with steel edges along the top so they can be ground without chipping. Benches are spaced so people can sit and watch. A painted line marks a walking path near the doors where boards are not allowed. Signs list the hours when skating is welcome.
look.prompt: Which concerns from the reading does this design answer, and which ones might still remain?

check.why: Liability is legal responsibility if someone is hurt.

check.q: Why do some skaters worry that a skatepark can become a fence?
choices: A city may ban skating everywhere else once a park exists.
Parks are always surrounded by tall metal fences.

Parks are only open to contest skaters.
check.why: Some skaters fear a park will be used as a reason to ban street skating.

check.q: What is a skate plaza?
choices: a parking lot where skating is banned

check.why: A skate plaza looks like an ordinary plaza but is built to be skated.

lessons.title: Bringing a Plan to the City
lessons.mainIdea: A strong skatepark proposal names a site, shows who will use it, answers stakeholders' concerns and keeps showing up.
reading: Many public skateparks began with a few skaters and a notebook. The first step is to learn who decides. In most towns that means a park district board or a city council, and their meetings are open to the public. Their agendas, the published lists of what will be discussed, show when public comment is allowed.

Next, gather evidence. Skaters can map where people ride now, count riders at popular spots on a few afternoons, and collect signatures from residents. A *petition* is a written request signed by many people. Letters from parents, teachers and business owners show that support goes beyond skaters themselves.

Then propose a site and answer concerns. A good site is visible, close to public transportation, near restrooms and away from homes that would hear the noise. Speakers should be ready for questions about cost, safety and upkeep. Groups such as The Skatepark Project publish guidance that local skaters can bring to officials.

Finally, expect a long process. Parks often take several years from the first meeting to the opening day. Skaters who keep attending, stay respectful and help with fundraising or design workshops build trust. That trust is often what turns a no into a yes.

words.d: a written request to a leader or government, signed by many people who support it
the published list of topics a council or board will discuss at a meeting
the part of a public meeting when residents may speak to the officials

look.title: Step by Step to a Park
look.text: Step 1: find out which board decides about parks. Step 2: read its agenda and note when public comment happens. Step 3: map where skaters ride and count them. Step 4: collect signatures and letters. Step 5: choose a site near transit and restrooms, away from homes. Step 6: speak, answer questions and return to the next meeting.
look.prompt: Which step do you think takes the most time, and what could a group of students do this month to start it?

check.q: What is an agenda?
choices: a signed letter from a parent
a drawing of a skatepark design
the published list of topics a council or board will discuss
a law that limits liability
check.why: An agenda lists what a meeting will cover, including when public comment happens.

check.q: Which is a good feature for a skatepark site?
choices: hidden behind buildings so no one sees it
right beside a hospital's bedrooms
on a busy road with no sidewalk
visible and close to transit and restrooms, away from homes
check.why: Visible sites near transit and restrooms, away from homes, answer common concerns.

check.q: Why does showing up again and again matter?
choices: Parks often take years, and steady, respectful attendance builds trust.
Councils vote only after a group attends ten times.
It lets skaters skip public comment.
It guarantees the park will open the next week.
check.why: The process is long, and trust built over time often changes the outcome.

review.q: Which best describes the purpose of a skate stopper?
choices: to slow skaters at the bottom of a ramp
to block grinding and sliding on an edge
to mark where a skatepark begins
to keep rain off a ledge
review.why: Skate stoppers break up an edge so boards cannot grind or slide along it.

review.q: Skate stoppers are one example of what larger idea?
choices: do-it-yourself building
heritage protection
hostile design
kinetic energy
review.why: Hostile design shapes public objects to stop certain uses.

review.q: What did the Long Live Southbank campaign achieve in 2014?
choices: a new skatepark under the Burnside Bridge
skateboarding's place in the Olympics
a ban on skate stoppers in London
an agreement to keep the undercroft for skating
review.why: In 2014 the campaign and the Southbank Centre agreed the undercroft would stay.

review.q: Which statement about Burnside is correct?
choices: Skaters began building it without permission in 1990, and the city later accepted it.
It was built by the city in the 1970s.
It sits beneath an arts center in London.
It was paid for by the Tony Hawk Foundation in 2002.
review.why: Burnside was skater-built starting in 1990 and later accepted by Portland.

review.q: A board stops at a knob, and the skater flies forward. Which idea explains this?
choices: heritage
inertia
liability
durometer
review.why: Inertia means the body keeps moving until a force stops it.

review.q: With v = 3 m/s and g = 9.8 m/s², waxing a ledge lowers μ from 0.5 to 0.2. What happens to the slide distance?
choices: It shrinks from about 2.3 m to about 0.92 m.
It stays the same because speed did not change.
It grows from about 0.92 m to about 2.3 m.
It doubles g to 19.6 m/s².

review.q: Why did the Tony Hawk Foundation change its name in 2020?
choices: because it stopped funding skateparks
because it merged with Long Live Southbank
because it moved to Kabul
to put the focus on parks and communities rather than one person
review.why: The Skatepark Project name centers the parks and communities.

review.q: Which is the strongest first step for students who want a public skatepark?
choices: find out which board decides and when public comment happens
pour concrete on an empty lot that night
add stoppers to the ledges they skate now
wait for a company to offer a park
review.why: Learning who decides and when residents may speak starts the civic process.
